reconcile.connective: Jamieson, Fausset, and Brown read Matthew's house as a later dwelling, not the birth stable, once Bethlehem's crowds had dispersed.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptics' Annotated Bible juxtaposes Luke's manger with Matthew's house as two flatly different settings, offering no bridging explanation.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, s.v. "Was Jesus born in a house or a manger?"
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "Was Jesus born in a house or a manger?" (skepticsannotatedbible.com/contra/manger.html)

excerpts.excerpt_text: And when they were come into the house—not the stable; for as soon as Bethlehem was emptied of its strangers, they would have no difficulty in finding a dwelling-house.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Explicitly denies Matthew's 'house' is the stable of the manger scene, explaining the different setting as the magi arriving after Bethlehem's census crowds had departed and lodging opened up.

pd_work.resource: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown, Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible (1871)
pd_work.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
pd_work.note: JFB treats Matthew 2:11 directly, arguing the magi found the family already relocated to a 'dwelling-house,' distinct from the stable/manger of Luke 2:7.

link.title: GotQuestions: Do the narratives of Jesus' birth contradict each other?
link.note: Notes Matthew 2:11's 'house' as the family's later Bethlehem lodging, after Luke's manger scene, assuming Joseph and Mary remained in Bethlehem after the birth.
